1:
Every witness marks the place before the sin. Gill derives Shittim from the acacia that grew there in the deserts of Arabia, gives its full name as Abel-Shittim, and notes it was Israel's last station, held until the death of Moses. Keil explains why this name rather than the other used for the same camp: it was at this northern point that Israel came into contact with Moab. Gill, Wesley and Henry all press the same aggravation, that the people fell here with Canaan in sight and the land almost in their hands, which Henry calls the highest treachery, to eat of idol sacrifices when they were about to be feasted on God's favours. Calvin takes it further back, that the people could bear prosperity no better than adversity: worn by fatigue or made impatient by famine they had rebelled before, and now, resting among fruitful fields in a habitable land, the easier life incites them to lasciviousness. Wesley adds that the daughters of Midian are meant as well as those of Moab, the two peoples being confederate in the design, and guesses the Moabite women are named because they began it, or because they were the greater persons, perhaps the relations or courtiers of Balak.

On how the trap worked they agree, and each contributes a step. Wesley observes that Moab, having failed by war and by witchcraft, tried familiarity instead; Gill describes the feasts kept on the parts of the sacrifice with every circumstance of pleasure, and thinks them peculiarly ensnaring to the young; Wesley adds that to share such a meal counted as sharing in the worship of the god it was offered to, and Henry presses that point through the apostle's argument against eating things offered to idols. Calvin sees a method in the order: the women did not solicit them to worship at once but invited them to banquets first, since Satan creeps on us by degrees, and had idolatry been named at the outset they might have refused. Henry states the same sequence as a rule, that those who have broken the fences of modesty will not be held by the bonds of piety. On the name they scatter. Gill lists derivations from prophecy, from an obscene posture, from the mountain, and from a deified lord, and reports Bedford for Mizraim and Calmet for Orus, which he refuses. Clarke and Wesley settle on the obscene sense; Calvin on the mountain, comparing the way an image is named for Loretto or Bologna; Ellicott alone identifies the god with Chemosh.

The sentence is where they divide. Clarke reads take all the heads as an order to assemble the chiefs and judges, hold an inquiry, and hang whoever is found guilty, and takes against the sun for the most public manner and in daylight; Wesley makes the heads themselves the culprits, chief both in the transgression and in place and power, singled out because their concurrence was the more mischievous. Calvin agrees they were hanged and gives the reason, that the lower sort died by the plague while the leaders went to the gallows so that the sight might awaken more terror; he rejects the alternative that Moses was only to fetch the princes to pass sentence, thinking it improbable that so vast a multitude were hanged, and turns the whole into a warning that a man in repute has the less excuse for the harm his example does. Ellicott declines to decide, laying out both constructions and noting only that the impaling followed the killing rather than caused it, and that the Greek uses the word rendered elsewhere to put to an open shame. Keil ends the section with the fact the others pass over: the order to the judges was never carried out, because the matter took a different turn.
6:
Keil sets the scene: while the heads were still deliberating and the congregation stood weeping before the tabernacle, a prince of Simeon brought a Midianite woman into the camp before the eyes of Moses and everyone. Calvin makes the timing the horror of it: amidst the tears of the pious, who trembled at the calamity they saw coming, this despiser of God led his harlot past them as though triumphing over shame itself. He adds that it can hardly be credited the thing was done after the judges had begun their work, so the account stands here to show how urgently chastisement was needed. Wesley reasons alike, that the man would not have run on certain ruin with the executions before his eyes. Henry counts the affronts: to the nation's justice, Zimri thinking himself too great for the judges to meddle with, and to its religion, coming among a fasting congregation to tell them in effect that he would fill the measure of sin as fast as they emptied it. Clarke enters the one dissent. Both parties were of chief families, which he thinks proves a marriage rather than prostitution, and he objects to the Vulgate for making the woman a harlot: the match was flatly against God's law, and there is no need to make it worse.

The word for the place they went into occurs nowhere else, and each reaches for a different parallel. Gill finds a near Arabic word which, with its article, gives the alcove of our own language, and notes it differed in shape and material from an ordinary tent, being of skins rather than hair or boughs; the Aruch calls it narrow above and broad below, a place where whores were put, and the Talmud uses it for a brothel. Ellicott offers two possibilities, the inner part of a common tent where the women lodged, or an arched tent of skins put up for the worship of Baal-peor, and records that the Greek renders it a furnace, the Latin a brothel; the phrase about the woman, he adds, may mean within her tent rather than through her belly, one word perhaps standing twice in the verse. Keil takes it for the arched inner part; Henry calls it a booth fitted up for lewdness. On the man who followed them in, Ellicott presses the grammar: the title the priest belongs to Aaron, not to Phinehas, since Eleazar held that office then, though Phinehas had civil as well as sacred authority.

Whether the act may be imitated is the question they all face. Clarke says he was inspired by the Spirit of the God of justice and that it can never be a precedent on any common occasion, then illustrates it from English history, calling such an act that of a zealot, useful at the time and justified only by the exigency. Henry removes the difficulty another way: Phinehas was heir to the high priesthood and so one of the judges Moses had commanded to kill the offenders, which leaves no countenance to a private man taking the magistrate's work out of his hand. Wesley agrees, adding that he acted in Moses's sight and by his consent. Calvin faces the objection squarely: Phinehas took up a sword God had not put in his hand. His answer is that a calling is not always confined to its ordinary office, and this was a special inspiration and not a rule, so whoever punishes a like crime in preposterous zeal boasts vainly of imitating him unless he is sure of the command, and should remember that ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of. On the twenty-four thousand against the apostle's twenty-three, Gill, Clarke, Wesley and Keil count a thousand hanged separately from the plague; Calvin and Ellicott prefer to call the figures round, or let the apostle's in one day account for it.
10:
The commendation turns on a possessive. Keil insists the phrase is not zeal for me but my zeal, the jealousy of Jehovah himself with which Phinehas was filled, so that in acting he restrained the very wrath that was working in the plague. Ellicott renders it in the same direction, that he was jealous with my jealousy, or displayed my jealousy. Calvin allows either reading, active or passive, that Phinehas was inflamed to vindicate God's glory or that he took God's own zeal upon him, and observes that on either construction God claims the deed as his own, making himself the author of the two deaths. Gill and Ellicott both stop on the repetition of the genealogy and give it the same purpose, that naming his father and grandfather marks him out as no private person but a man clothed with public authority; Gill adds a second reason, that it shows him heir apparent to the high priesthood, and that so far from barring him from it the act confirms it to him.

Calvin then guards the word atonement against a use he expects. When God declares himself appeased by the punishment, we are not to imagine a meritorious satisfaction of the kind by which he says the Papists pretend their penalties are redeemed: the just chastisement of sin may be a sacrifice of sweet savour, but it is no expiation and no compensation. What happened was that a wrath fanned into flame by the people's ungodliness was checked when the ungodliness was checked. He presses the point from the Psalm, where the atonement is ascribed not to the act but to the prayer, since Phinehas by right of his priesthood interceded; and he adds Paul's rule that those who judge themselves are not judged. Keil describes the grant in the same legal terms as the giving of a covenant, that is, the fulfilling of it, and stresses that the form is irrevocable, since God never breaks a covenant he has made. Calvin meets an objection here too. If Phinehas was already his father's undoubted successor by law, what did he gain? That God often declares as a reward what he has already freely promised, as the blessing given to Abraham before Isaac was born is repeated after he was ready to offer him.

What the everlasting priesthood covers, and for how long, divides them. Wesley reads the covenant of peace from the effect and from the office, since Phinehas made peace between God and the people and the priest's whole business is to mediate; but he holds the promise conditional, made void by the miscarriages of Phinehas's sons, transferred to Eli of Ithamar's line, made void again, and restored in Solomon's day. Clarke takes peace for prosperity in both worlds, and insists the everlasting priesthood means Christ's, of which Aaron's was the shadow, no matter what family held the office; then he counts the succession, twelve high priests of this race to Solomon, nine more to the captivity, fifteen thereafter, with Ithamar's family holding it some hundred and fifty years before Zadok restored it. Ellicott gives the same history more briefly and adds the interruption under Eli and the joint priesthood in David's time. Calvin denies there was any real break, inferring that Zadok as well as Abiathar came of Phinehas. On what the covenant finally means, Gill reads it of Christ and his spiritual seed, with whom it stands fast, and Ellicott follows him almost word for word, adding that it was made by the blood of the cross.
14:
The two names are recorded, and Calvin explains why: as the memory of the just is blessed, so it was fitting that the author of so foul a sin be condemned to perpetual infamy. He notices that part of the shame falls on the whole tribe, which was not itself charged with the offence, and takes it as a lesson that a man should sharply correct any relative he sees going wrong, that being the true way to honour his own blood. Both parties being of noble family teaches two things at once, that God's judgment is no respecter of rank, and that the higher a man stands the more conspicuous his disgrace. Ellicott suspects the tribe of Simeon was deeply implicated and its members the chief sufferers in the plague, and corrects both titles from the Hebrew, reading a father's house for a chief house and making Zur head of the communities of a father's house rather than of a people; Zur appears later as one of the five kings of Midian whom Israel killed. Gill supplies the legends: the Samaritan Chronicle makes her a king's daughter who enticed the prince to eat her food and worship her idols, and the Targum calls her Selonae and daughter of Balak. Calvin refuses to settle where she was raised, thinking the question unimportant.

Why Midian is named and not Moab is the question the section raises, and four answers are given. Gill says Israel had been forbidden to war on Moab, spared for the sake of Lot their ancestor and, as Jarchi adds, of Ruth who was to come from them; but the Midianites first sent for Balaam, kept him after Balak dismissed him, and seem to have received the wicked counsel from him. Wesley says simply that they were the guiltier party, in fetching Balaam, in receiving him, and in contriving the means. Ellicott rejects the descent argument outright: it cannot rest on Moab's descent from Lot, since the Midianites were themselves descendants of Abraham and ought for that reason to have feared his God and shown kindness to their kindred. He prefers to say the measure of Moab's sin was not yet full, and observes that Moab did not escape either, being shut out of the congregation to the tenth generation. Calvin declines all of it. No good reason appears why God should bear with one nation and hasten to punish the other, and we should revere his judgments rather than discuss them further than is lawful.

On the order itself Henry draws a distinction: God punished Israel with a plague, as a father corrects his own children with a rod, but no Midianite is said to have died of it, and they were punished instead by the sword of an enemy. He notes that Moses, the meekest of men, is commanded to vex them, and makes the rule that we must set ourselves against whatever occasions sin to us, though it be a right eye or a right hand, since whatever draws us to sin should be a vexation like a thorn in the flesh. Calvin faces the harder problem, that God elsewhere forbids revenge. His answer is that God, the just avenger, uses men as the lawful ministers of his vengeance, so what is condemned is only the revenge carnal passion drives men to, while a man moved by well-regulated zeal pleads not his own cause but God's. Keil states the ground flatly, that they were to be smitten for the stratagem they had practised. Gill and Wesley both stress the word wiles rather than wars, Wesley remarking that under pretence of kindred and friendship, instead of the war Israel expected, they sought only to insinuate themselves and work their plot. Clarke points forward to the execution, twelve thousand Israelites destroying the cities and the five kings.
